name: Bolt
baseline: Lua 5.4 (PUC-Rio). The same charts also include Luau, LuaJIT with the JIT off (-joff), Lua 5.1 and 5.3, Wren, Python 3.9 and 2.7, and Node with --jitless.
workload: Ten interpreter-only micro-benchmarks: fib(30), 10M-iteration closure iterator, 256x256 Mandelbrot (255 iterations), Vec2 create/add/distance object benchmarks, binary_tree(4, 12), spectral(500), nbody(500000) and fannkuch(9).
claimed_speedup: Versus Lua 5.4 (chart values, ms, lower is better): fib(30) 52 vs 62; closure iterator 188 vs 300; Mandelbrot 87 vs 184; Vec2 create-create-add 39 (14 with mimalloc) vs 85; Vec2 add 12.7 (4.7 with mimalloc) vs 26.0; Vec2 distance 31 vs 96; binary_tree 274 vs 339; spectral 376 vs 471; nbody 744 vs 1097. Slower on fannkuch(9): 281 vs 148. Ratios are derived from page data (about 1.2x on fib to 3.1x on Vec2 distance).
compiler_and_flags: Bolt built with MSVC using the CMake configuration in the repo (flags not quoted in the doc). Other languages built to their recommended instructions or taken as prebuilt binaries, whichever was faster; no flags given.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, 32 GB DDR4-3200 in dual channel
tradeoffs: A different language, not Lua source-compatible: statically type-checked, 8-byte NaN-boxed values, register VM, embed-first C API. No tail-call optimisation. The compiler is described as early stage. Allocation-heavy results depend on the allocator (system allocator versus mimalloc).
caveats: First-party benchmark. The numbers are bar-chart images in the doc (read from the PNGs, not from text); averages of 10 or 15 runs with no pinning stated. Bolt is slower than Lua 5.4 on fannkuch(9), and Luau beats Bolt on binary_tree, nbody and fannkuch. Only interpreters are compared (JIT-enabled runtimes excluded except LuaJIT -joff). The Lua 5.4 minor version and the baseline build flags are not stated, which is why this is not tier A despite public benchmark code and a named CPU. Bolt was built on Windows with MSVC.
found_via: WebSearch 'Show HN new embeddable scripting language C++ faster than Lua 2026 benchmark fib' surfaced the HN post 'Show HN: Bolt'; opened github.com/Beariish/bolt and its doc/Bolt Performance.md, then read the chart PNGs.

name: gkurt/quickjs (performance-optimised QuickJS-NG fork)
baseline: Upstream quickjs-ng master (QuickJS-NG, the maintained fork of Bellard's QuickJS)
workload: A CI workflow builds the fork and upstream quickjs-ng in Release mode and runs Octane 2.0, upstream tests/microbench.js and bench/runtime.js (with cachegrind instruction counts), alternating sides for 3 runs each and comparing medians.
claimed_speedup: PR #8 comparison workflow: Octane total score 2022 to 2385 (+18%); microbench 1.18x faster (geomean); runtime benchmarks 1.57x faster with instructions down 35%. Later PR #9: +22.1% geomean on Octane over the previous fork head. PR #12: 22 benchmarks faster and none slower, wall-clock geomean down 22%, instructions down 21% over 23 benchmarks.
compiler_and_flags: Release build via the repo's build; compiler and flags not stated on the pages read
hardware: GitHub Actions Linux/X64 runner; CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (personal fork of quickjs-ng, 3.9k stars upstream)
tradeoffs: Same C API and engine as QuickJS-NG. Adds inline caches, dense-array fast paths, cached global slots, computed-goto regexp execution and similar. Octane peak memory rose 18% in the PR #8 comparison (mostly CodeLoad and PdfJS); PR #9 reports +1.6% geomean peak memory; PR #12 reports memory mostly slightly lower.
caveats: Numbers come from PR descriptions and the fork's own CI workflow, not an independent run. The fork is days to weeks old (PRs merged 2026-09-25 and 2026-09-29), has no stars and branch names indicate AI-assisted work (claude/...). The baseline is upstream quickjs-ng, not Bellard's QuickJS. PR #12 states test262 shows 14 errors out of 82220, the same 14 as upstream's list. No indication the changes were proposed upstream.
found_via: WebSearch 'QuickJS fork performance improvements faster than upstream QuickJS Octane score C engine github' surfaced the fork's pull requests; opened github.com/gkurt/quickjs, its commits page and PRs 8, 9 and 12.

name: GNU Guile
baseline: Lua 5.4.7 (PUC-Rio). The same table also lists LuaJIT 2.1.1, Janet 1.36.0 and Tcl 9.0.0.
workload: Naive recursive fibonacci fib(47) = 2,971,215,073, run as 'guile fib.scm' and 'lua fib.lua', average of 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: 102.887 s for Guile 3.0.10 versus 203.702 s for Lua 5.4.7, about 2.0x faster (derived from page data). LuaJIT at 37.837 s is faster than both; Janet (479.663 s) and Tcl (2230.883 s) are slower.
compiler_and_flags: Interpreters installed by apt/asdf in an ubuntu:24.04 Docker image (guile 3.0.10, lua 5.4.7); the README states only common release flags for compiled languages and gives none for the interpreters
hardware: Hetzner CCX23, 4 vCPU, 'Intel Xeon 3.1Ghz' (exact model not stated), 16 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04
stars_or_usage: Mirror has 0 stars; the benchmark repo drujensen/fib has 906 stars. Guile is the GNU project extension language.
tradeoffs: Scheme, not Lua-like; garbage-collected library meant for embedding with a C API; LGPL linking terms; larger runtime and longer start-up than Lua.
caveats: Single naive-recursion micro-benchmark, so it says little about general scripting workloads. The benchmark was last run 2024-12-05. The repo URL is the unofficial GitHub mirror (last commit shown 2022-04-08); the canonical repository is on savannah.gnu.org, which was not reachable, so maintenance status is unknown and the upstream project is believed active. Benchmark code and Dockerfile are public but the CPU model is only 'Intel Xeon'.
found_via: Lead in data/wave12/leads.md (drujensen/fib); WebSearch 'Janet OR Guile OR s7 OR Chibi embeddable scheme interpreter benchmark versus Lua faster fib' also returned the repo; opened its README and the Guile mirror page.

name: LibJS (Ladybird browser JavaScript engine)
baseline: Duktape 2.99.99 on Ubuntu and macOS (QuickJS 2026.06.04 is faster than LibJS in the same suite)
workload: Eight tests from Mozilla's arewefastyet v8-v7 benchmark (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes), scores summed, run by the project's GitHub Actions on 2026-10-05.
claimed_speedup: Ubuntu score 691 versus Duktape 489 (about 1.4x, derived from page data); macOS arm64 1169 versus Duktape 905 (about 1.3x). QuickJS scores 1217 on Ubuntu and 1761 on macOS, so LibJS is slower than QuickJS. No Windows row for ladybird.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu and macos-arm64 runners; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: LibJS lives inside the Ladybird browser tree (inherited from SerenityOS), not packaged as a small standalone embeddable library; the benchmarked executable is 43.8 MB on Ubuntu versus 1 MB for QuickJS. Targets full ECMAScript conformance.
caveats: Third-party CI suite without stated flags or CPU model. LibJS is slower than Duktape on some individual tests (RegExp on Ubuntu: 66 versus 129) and faster on others (Crypto 1025 versus 783). It beats only Duktape, not QuickJS, among the listed baselines.
found_via: Opened ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark README (via raw.githubusercontent.com) found through the embedded-JS WebSearch; compared every engine in its Ubuntu and macOS score rows against Duktape and QuickJS; opened github.com/LadybirdBrowser/ladybird and its commits page.

name: Bare (Holepunch JavaScript runtime)
baseline: QuickJS 2026.06.04 and Duktape (2.99.99 on Ubuntu and macOS, 2.7.0 on Windows)
workload: Eight tests from Mozilla's arewefastyet v8-v7 benchmark (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes), scores summed, run by GitHub Actions on 2026-10-05.
claimed_speedup: Ubuntu score 41468 versus QuickJS 1217 and Duktape 489; macOS arm64 40758 versus QuickJS 1761 and Duktape 905; Windows 36041 versus QuickJS 1067 and Duktape 371. That is about 23x to 34x QuickJS (derived from page data). The gain comes from the V8 JIT.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu, macos-arm64 and windows runners; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Embeddable through a C API (include/bare.h) with libuv, but it wraps V8 through the libjs abstraction, so footprint is large (64.6 MB on Ubuntu versus 1 MB for QuickJS). Peer-to-peer runtime with its own module system.
caveats: A JIT engine against interpreters, so the comparison says nothing about Bare's own code beating QuickJS or Duktape. Third-party CI suite without stated flags or CPU model. The engine behind the benchmarked build is taken from the repository page (V8 by default), not from the suite page. Overlaps conceptually with the V8 entry.
found_via: Opened ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark README via the embedded-JS WebSearch; read the Bare row against QuickJS and Duktape; opened github.com/holepunchto/bare and its commits page.

name: AngelScript
baseline: Duktape (version not stated; the same table lists PUC Lua at 1.341 s, where this engine is slower)
workload: Recursive fibonacci test (tests/fib.*) run as a separate process through the repo's bench.exe, wall time including process start-up averaged over 5 runs, July 2015 snapshot.
claimed_speedup: 2.039 s versus Duktape 9.544 s, about 4.7x faster than Duktape (derived from page data); slower than PUC Lua at 1.341 s (about 1.5x, derived from page data). The scriptorium table also lists an AngelScript JIT variant at 1.859 s.
compiler_and_flags: VS2015 RC where possible, VS2013 elsewhere, linked statically; per-engine flags not stated
hardware: AMD A10 3.8 GHz (exact model not stated), 8 GiB RAM, Windows 7 64-bit
stars_or_usage: 286 stars; packaged as vcpkg port 'angelscript' and Conan Center recipe 'angelscript'
tradeoffs: Statically typed C++-like script language with a C++ registration API; the official GitHub repository replaced the older SVN mirror (codecat/angelscript-mirror, archived 2025-08-14).
caveats: Eleven-year-old snapshot (July 2015) on one recursive-fib test; the author says 'Take it with a grain of salt'. Timings include process start-up and vary between logged runs (bench.csv shows Duktape from 9.06 s to 14.3 s). The Duktape version is not stated and is much older than current releases, and PUC Lua (1.341 s in the same table) is faster than this engine. Scriptorium is an archived repository with no per-engine build flags. A separate April 2026 benchmark (sashi0034/script-language-benchmark, Windows, MSVC 2022 Release, author notes the code was generated with Codex) has AngelScript faster than Lua on 7 of 16 workloads (float2string, mandelbrot, native_loop by 0.3%, particles_kinematics, queen, sha256, spectral_norm) and slower on 9 (for example dictionary 20.9 versus 4.0, sort 329 versus 6.2, fibonacci_loop 52.9 versus 26.9); units are not stated.

name: MicroQuickJS (MQuickJS)
baseline: QuickJS (Bellard); the README is the only comparison and gives no QuickJS numbers
workload: Not measured against QuickJS in the README; the README describes running JavaScript in as little as 10 kB of RAM with about 100 kB of ROM (ARM Thumb-2 code including the C library) and references 'make microbench' and an Octane run.
claimed_speedup: No speed-up claimed: 'The speed is comparable to QuickJS.' Memory claim without a QuickJS figure: programs run in as little as 10 kB of RAM, whole engine about 100 kB ROM.
tradeoffs: Supports only a stricter ES5-like subset of JavaScript; tracing compacting GC, no dependency on malloc, UTF-8 strings, standard library lives in ROM so instantiation is nearly free. C API similar to QuickJS but not compatible.
caveats: No numbers for QuickJS are given, so the memory advantage is not quantified, and speed is stated to be merely comparable. Included as the single notable tier D entry for the memory-footprint claim; the benchmark inputs (QuickJS microbench, patched Octane) are only available from a separate tarball that was not opened.
